title: Deprecation gaps: the superseded-route table has no guard, and Trust Task URIs have no deprecation path at all
body:
Two gaps in how this workspace retires things, both surfaced while retiring `vta/discovery/capabilities/1.0` (#1043, #1044). Neither is urgent; both get worse the more we retire, and the direction of travel is clearly toward retiring more.

## 1. The superseded-route table has no guard

`deprecation.rs` maps legacy REST routes to the Trust Task that supersedes them, and its purpose is explicit:

> removal can be gated on **observed usage dropping to zero** rather than a guessed calendar date

#1042 deleted `GET /capabilities` and left its row in `SUPERSEDED` behind. The row matched a path that could never be hit again, so it would have read **zero usage forever** — which is precisely the signal the table exists to produce. It was removed by hand in #1044, having been noticed by accident.

**Nothing ties that table to the live router.** No test asserts every `(method, path)` in `SUPERSEDED` is a route the service actually serves, so a dangling row is silent, and a silent dangling row makes the metric say "safe to delete" about something already deleted.

### Requested

A test that walks the assembled router (`build_api_router` already exists and the OpenAPI assertions already introspect it) and asserts every `SUPERSEDED` entry corresponds to a live route. Failure text should say which way to fix it: if the route is gone, drop the row; if the row is a typo, correct it — do not delete the row to silence the test, because the row is what carries the successor URI.

Note the reverse direction is *not* wanted: a live route absent from the table is legitimate, and `deprecation.rs` already documents which routes are deliberately excluded and why.

## 2. There is no deprecation path for a Trust Task URI

`deprecation.rs` gives REST routes the full treatment — `Deprecation: true`, a `Link: rel="successor-version"` header, and a per-route hit counter, so removal is evidence-led.

**Trust Task URIs get none of it.** A task can be retired only by deleting it, and the only available evidence is a source audit: grep this repo and the ones we can see, and reason about the rest.

That is what #1044 did, and it was stated plainly there as the weaker instrument it is. It was defensible for that task — zero consumers anywhere, plus a member whose vocabulary corresponded to nothing — but it does not generalise. The next retirement may be one someone *is* calling, and we would find out from a support ticket.

### Requested

The Trust-Task equivalent of the REST mechanism:

- A `SUPERSEDED_TASKS` table — `(retired URI, successor URI, reason)`.
- The dispatch spine increments a counter, labelled by URI, when a retired task is dispatched, and includes the successor in the response so a client can act rather than guess. The Trust-Task error shape already carries a machine-readable code, so there is somewhere to put it.
- Retirement then follows the same rule as routes: delete on an observed zero.

Worth checking against the framework spec first — a deprecation signal may already be defined for Trust Tasks, in which case this is adoption rather than invention. That was the outcome for capability negotiation itself (#1042): `trust-task-discovery/0.1` already existed and we simply were not serving it.

### Interaction with the census

`UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` and `vtc-service`'s `UNPUBLISHED_CANONICAL_OK` both shrink monotonically by test, and #1044 showed a URI can leave those lists by *ceasing to exist* rather than by gaining a spec. A deprecation table would make that path explicit rather than inferred from a count that moved.

title: vta-service-v0.20.0
body:
### Added

- **discovery**: Serve canonical capability negotiation, drop the parallel REST route ([#1042](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1042))

* feat(discovery)!: serve canonical capability negotiation, drop the parallel REST route

  Clients had no way to ask a VTA which Trust Tasks it serves. Calling one it does
  not is a 30-second DIDComm timeout with no explanation — the failure mode
  `didhosting-083-retired-task-uris` describes.

  The answer already existed and we were not serving it. `trust-task-discovery/0.1`
  is a published family in the dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf registry, carried by the
  `trust-tasks-rs` we already depend on: a client sends slug-glob patterns (`*`,
  `acl/*`, or an exact slug) and gets back the Type URIs the responder serves plus
  the framework version it targets. Nothing needed inventing, and — unusually for a
  new family — nothing needed specifying upstream first.

  The VTA answers **from its own dispatch table**. `dispatched_uris()` was already
  generated by `dispatch_table!` from the same declarations that build the match
  arms; it is now available at runtime rather than only under `cfg(test)`. A
  hand-maintained list would be a second source of truth, and an overstated
  discovery response is worse than none: a client believes a task is available and
  finds out on a live call.

  **What this does not do.** It answers "do we both know this task, at this
  version". It does not answer "do we agree how its payload is spelled" — two peers
  can both serve `contexts/create/1.0` and still disagree about `basePath` vs
  `base_path`, which is what #1033 was. Said plainly on the SDK method, because the
  obvious misreading is that discovery makes wire skew detectable.

title: docs: design note for Trust Task version negotiation and its versioning contract
body:
Refs #1045. **Design only** — no code, no URIs, nothing dispatched.

Adds `docs/05-design-notes/task-version-negotiation.md` and indexes it.

## The problem, live rather than hypothetical

A client sends whatever version it was compiled against:

```rust
self.dispatch_trust_task(trust_tasks::TASK_VAULT_LIST_0_1, filters, VAULT_TT_TIMEOUT)
```

`vault/list` is published at **0.1, 0.2 and 0.3**. This VTA serves 0.1 and 0.2. A client built against 0.3 gets `unsupported_type` — over DIDComm, a 30-second timeout with no explanation.

Everything needed to fix it already exists and is unused: discovery (#1042) says what a peer serves, `TypeUri` decomposes `(slug, major, minor)`. What is missing is the client choosing.

## Negotiation and versioning are one decision

Which is why they are one note. **Negotiation is tractable if and only if versions carry a compatibility contract** — without one, "negotiate" cannot mean better than "match exactly or fail".

### The contract: 1.0 is unremarkable

The notation is already semver. What is missing is a *promise*.

`vault/list` 0.1 and 0.3 have **identical payload shapes**. The only difference is enum values — `oauth-tokens` → `oauthTokens`. A breaking wire change shipped as a minor bump, twice.

**That is not a semver violation.** `0.x` explicitly guarantees nothing, so the registry is following semver correctly; semver at 0.x simply promises nothing to build on.

Proposed: drop the exemption. MAJOR for any wire-visible change that is not purely additive, MINOR for additive-only. A family at `7.2` is fine. No grammar change, no flag day — the rule binds the *next* change.

### Why not `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`

Considered and rejected. It is a framework grammar change — `TypeUri::parse_version` splits once and parses the remainder as `u32`, so `1.2.3` does not parse, and changing that touches SPEC §6.1 for every task in the registry.

The substantive objection is different: **a PATCH component carries no negotiation value and costs identity.** If PATCH is invisible on the wire then `1.2.3` and `1.2.4` are byte-identical — yet any matcher comparing Type URIs sees two different tasks. The URI *is* the wire identity.

And under the variant where MINOR is breaking too, a negotiator must match `MAJOR.MINOR` exactly — which is today's behaviour, for an extra component.

## The part I think is the good bit

**The sender speaks down**, and that resolves what looks like a hard conflict.

The payload schemas are `additionalProperties: false` and the generated types carry `deny_unknown_fields`. So a new client sending a new optional member to an old server is **rejected, not ignored** — which appears to rule out additive minors entirely.

It does not, because **nobody ever sends up-version**:

- Old client → new server: accepted, everything added since was optional. ✓
- New client → old server: would break — **but never happens**, the sender negotiated down first. ✓

So negotiation removes the need for forward tolerance, and `deny_unknown_fields` **stays**. That matters: it is a security requirement in CLAUDE.md, and #656/#658 are the scar where a silently-accepted unknown member minted a super-admin. Buying forward compatibility by tolerating unknown members would have given that up.

## What the note is careful about

- **The algorithm mirrors transport selection**, which CLAUDE.md already defines — intersect, take the highest common, typed error on empty, never silently downgrade. Consistency rather than invention.
- **The cost is stated**: negotiating down to 1.1 means holding a 1.1 encoder. The additive-only rule is what bounds it — bridging an additive minor is *dropping* members, not rewriting them. Contrast `wire_v0_2`, which rewrites enum values and has to carve out signed payloads because mutating those bytes voids the proof.
- **The rule needs teeth.** A minor bump is mechanically checkable against published schemas (added members optional, none removed, no enum-value changes). That census belongs upstream with the schemas.
- **What it does not solve**: two peers can both serve `contexts/create/1.0` and still disagree about `basePath` vs `base_path` (#1033). Discovery and negotiation do not make wire skew detectable.
- **Startup and staleness**: negotiation must not block boot (`server::run` has to reach its shutdown select), and a cached result must be able to go stale — R6.2, no latched status.

## Scope

§3 (negotiation) is entirely ours — client behaviour over an already-published discovery task.

§2 (the contract) is a **registry decision**. `vault/*`, `acl/*`, `keys/*` are canonical families in `trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`, and the deliberate direction since #840 has been to fold onto them, which means inheriting their versioning rules. The note flags checking the framework for existing versioning semantics before proposing anything — twice now the answer to "should we build this" has been "it already exists upstream and we were not using it", most recently `trust-task-discovery/0.1`.

## Four open questions (§6)

1. Ship negotiation first against exact-match semantics, or wait for the contract?
2. Negotiate every family, or only the five published at more than one version?
3. Empty intersection at startup — refuse to connect, or degrade to what did negotiate? The transport precedent refuses; a task surface is more granular.
4. Does `spec/vta/*` adopt the contract ahead of the registry, and what does being stricter than the families we fold onto mean?

Docs-only; no crate source touched, so no version bump.

MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH was considered and rejected. It is a framework grammar change
(`parse_version` splits once and parses the remainder as u32, so `1.2.3` does not
parse), and more substantively a PATCH component carries no negotiation value: if
it is invisible on the wire then `1.2.3` and `1.2.4` are byte-identical, yet any
matcher comparing Type URIs sees two different tasks. The URI is the wire
identity. And with MINOR breaking too, a negotiator would have to match
`MAJOR.MINOR` exactly — today's behaviour, for an extra component.

## Why the sender speaks down

The negotiated minor is the LOWER of the two and the sender encodes at it. That
is what makes this work against the schemas as they stand, and it resolves what
looks like a conflict.

The payload schemas are `additionalProperties: false` and the generated types
carry `deny_unknown_fields` — so a new client sending a new optional member to an
old server would be rejected, not ignored. That looks like it rules out additive
minors. It does not, because nobody ever sends up-version: negotiation removes
the need for forward tolerance entirely, and `deny_unknown_fields` stays. It is a
security requirement here, and #656/#658 are the scar where a silently-accepted
unknown member minted a super-admin.

## Not ours alone

§3 (negotiation) is client behaviour over an already-published discovery task and
is entirely ours. §2 (the contract) is a registry decision — `vault/*`, `acl/*`
and `keys/*` are canonical families in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf, and
folding onto them means inheriting their versioning rules. The note says which is
which, and flags that the framework should be checked for existing versioning
semantics before anything is proposed: twice now the answer to "should we build
this" has been "it already exists upstream and we were not using it".

Design only. No code, no URIs, nothing dispatched.

Refs #1045

title: Add the VDC (verifiable delegation credential) as a DTG edge credential
body:
## Problem

All six credential types in WD01 are **attestations** — each states that something is true about the graph, and a verifier evaluates it as a claim. Not one of them establishes that one entity may **act in another's name**. The VIC comes closest, but it is onboarding-shaped: its subject is by definition not yet in the graph, it is short-lived, and §Security says treat it as single-use.

Meanwhile delegation is already assumed by the specification's own vocabulary, with nothing to express it:

- `spec/terms-definitions/persona.md` — an identity controlled by the person "or their delegate"
- `spec/terms-definitions/personal_network_vault.md` — a person "may sometimes choose to delegate use of their credentials or keys to a VTA"
- `spec/intro.md` — AI agents are first-class DTG nodes, and an Agent Card VDS is planned

So today we can say "person P and agent A have a relationship" (VRC), but not "A may act in P's name, for these acts, until this date, and P can withdraw it."

## Delegation, not authority

The VDC is deliberately confined to **delegation**, and the PR adds an informative subsection, *Delegation and Authority*, saying so:

| Question | Answered by | The act is attributed to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| May this party do this thing, as itself? | authority — not defined in this specification | the party itself |
| May this party act in another's name? | delegation — the VDC | the entity in whose name it acts |

Neither implies the other. A service granted access to a person's mailbox may read that mail as itself; it has not thereby been appointed to send mail in that person's name. Conversely, a delegate appointed to correspond in a person's name holds that appointment whether or not it has access to any particular mailbox — and where it has not, the appointment gets it nowhere.

Two consequences are stated normatively:

- **A VDC never supplies authority.** A delegate cannot do in the delegator's name what the delegator could not do itself. A verifier must settle both questions separately, and a valid VDC is never on its own sufficient grounds to proceed (Security Considerations item 9).
- **The word "authority" is left free.** If the WG later wants a verifiable authority credential, it can be defined without reinterpreting the VDC or contending with it for the same semantic ground.

The subsection ends with a *when to use a VDC* test in the same style as the spec's existing credential/artifact test: **ask whose name the act is performed in.** The actor's own → a question of authority, not this credential. Another entity's, with the act attributed to that entity → delegation, and the VDC is what establishes it.

## How a delegation composes with authority

A second informative subsection answers the question a reviewer asks immediately after the first: if a VDC is not authority, does the delegate need authority of its own, or has the delegator handed its own over?

Neither. **A VDC moves the question; it does not answer it.** A verifier substitutes the delegator for the delegate and then asks the question it would have asked of the delegator directly. Three checks, each independent:

1. **Is this the delegate, and may it act in the delegator's name for this act?** — the VDC, plus chain and invocation binding. Defined here.
2. **May the delegator perform this act?** — membership, governance, an IDVC, a permission credential, verifier policy. Not defined here, and a VDC does not influence its outcome.
3. **Must the delegate independently qualify?** — a governance determination, now stated as such in §Governance Considerations.

The reach of a delegation is the **intersection** of what the delegator may do and what the VDC chain appoints the delegate for — never the union, and never more than either. Three consequences are spelled out:

- **Nothing the delegator holds is copied to the delegate.** A credential issued to the delegator stays the delegator's; the issuer's assurance about the delegator does not extend to the delegate, and a delegator cannot re-issue what it was itself issued. Delegation is a statement about who may speak in one's name, not a transfer of anything received.
- **Withdrawing the delegator's own permission stops the delegate immediately**, without revoking the VDC, because check 2 is evaluated at the time of the act. Revoking the VDC and withdrawing the underlying permission are different remedies with different reach.
- **A `scope` may exceed what the delegator itself may do**, which is not an error given that permissions change over the life of a durable appointment. Verifiers MUST NOT treat it as conferring anything beyond check 2; issuers SHOULD NOT do it.

This also rules out the alternative reading — a VDC as a container the delegator fills with its own permissions and hands over. That would make every issued authorization transferable by its holder, break the issuer's revocation reach, and attribute the act to the delegate rather than the delegator, which is the opposite of what delegation means.

## Why a new type rather than an existing one

Each overload fails, and the failures are informative:

- **VEC** — its `endorsement` object is community-defined and the spec explicitly says verifiability applies to the signature "not to the truth of the assertions." Putting representation inside a container whose stated semantics are *unverified opinion* means a verifier cannot distinguish "is good at Rust" from "may act as me."
- **VIC** — the least-bad overload, but its rules are terminal and onboarding-shaped, per above. Reusing it would mean redefining it.
- **VRC + a relationship-type field** — VRC currently carries no payload beyond `issuer` and `credentialSubject.id`. Adding semantics changes it from a bare edge to a typed one, which cuts against the ZKP predicate story, and imposes the bidirectional-pair requirement and the "new unique R-DID per counterparty" MUST on something inherently asymmetric.

The underlying reason is that a verifier evaluates an attestation by asking whether it is *true*. Representation asks something else — whether this party may stand in for that one, for this act, right now — and answering it requires scope containment, chain resolution, invocation binding and timely revocation. A distinct type string is what forces a verifier onto that path rather than the claim-evaluation one.

## What this PR does

Adds `DelegationCredential` (**VDC**) as a seventh concrete subtype and third edge credential.

**Applies the specification's own test.** §Credentials versus Trust Task Artifacts splits delegation cleanly, and the PR states this explicitly:

- the **grant** — "P appointed A to act in its name, for scope S, until T" — is true standing alone → credential, defined here
- the **invocation** — "A is acting in P's name, now, to do X" — is meaningful only in-exchange → trust task artifact, left to the DTG Core Trust Task Protocols spec

**Edge, with consent.** A grant plus a matching acceptance forms the edge, consistent with VRC/VMC pairing. A grant alone establishes what the delegator appointed, not what the delegate agreed to. This is the same consent question as #8 / #12 and is defined here in the same shape, without pre-empting that discussion.

**The machinery the six types do not have:**

- `delegation.scope` (REQUIRED, non-empty) — the acts the delegate may perform in the delegator's name; vocabulary governed by the VTC/VTN, exactly as VEC's `endorsement` is
- `delegation.parent` / `maxDepth` — attenuation-only re-delegation; a chain must resolve to a root delegation issued by the principal in whose name the acts would ultimately be performed. `parent` reuses the VWC `digest` encoding (SHA-256 over JCS) rather than introducing a second convention
- **Invocation binding** — a VDC is not a bearer token; the delegate must demonstrate key control at request time
- `validUntil` REQUIRED — an appointment with no expiry cannot be reasoned about by a verifier that cannot reach the delegator
- `credentialStatus` REQUIRED — see the note below

**Security considerations added:** misreading a VDC as a claim, treating a delegation as a permission, chain escalation, revocation latency, bearer use, and personhood laundering. The last is worth flagging on its own: a PHC asserts one membership per real person, and because a delegate's acts are attributable to the delegator, a verifier that cannot distinguish the two may credit several agents of one person as several people.

**Privacy considerations added:** delegation correlation (prefer R-DIDs), and scope terms as identifiers.

**Prior art:** ZCAP-LD and UCAN are cited in an informative subsection. The VDC reuses their *mechanics* — attenuation, root resolution, invocation binding — while noting the semantics differ: those models chain permissions, the VDC chains representation. It expresses those mechanics natively rather than embedding an opaque token, because scope is precisely the payload holders need to prove over in zero knowledge.

## Note on `credentialStatus`

`credentialStatus` currently appears **nowhere** in the specification. §Security Considerations tells verifiers to "check applicable revocation status via the governing trust registry," but no property tells them where to look. For attestations that is survivable; for a delegation — where revocation is the delegator's only means of withdrawing an appointment already made — it is not.

This PR therefore makes `credentialStatus` REQUIRED on the VDC only, and deliberately does not touch §Base Structure. The spec-wide question is worth its own issue and I'm happy to raise it separately.

## Also updated

Abstract, intro, taxonomy diagram and type hierarchy, `dtg_edge_credential` term (two subtypes → three), `specs.json` description, and a new `verifiable_delegation_credential` term definition. `CONTEXT.md` gains VDC and delegation-vs-authority language entries.

Renders clean with `npm run render`: no unresolved term references, all JSON examples parse, and the only dangling definitions reported are the five pre-existing ones.

## Open questions for the WG

1. **Scope vocabulary** — left entirely to VTC/VTN governance, mirroring VEC. Should the core spec instead define a minimal baseline so cross-community delegation is meaningful?
2. **A companion authority credential** — this PR reserves the ground rather than filling it. Is a verifiable authority credential wanted, and if so should the two be specified together so the boundary is drawn once?
3. **Delegate eligibility** — check 3 above is left to governance. Should the core spec instead take a position, e.g. requiring that a delegate acting within a community hold a VMC of its own?
4. **Acceptance strictness** — this draft requires the acceptance for a *complete edge* but lets a verifier rely on a grant alone where delegate consent isn't material. Should acceptance be unconditionally REQUIRED?
5. **`maxDepth` default** — this draft prohibits re-delegation when `maxDepth` is absent. Fail-closed seems right; confirming it is intended.
6. **ZKP constructions** — a delegation predicate is added to the list in §Zero-Knowledge and Selective Disclosure, but the constructions themselves are not worked out. Likely interacts with #9.
7. **Naming** — VDC is free, but sits close to VDS (verifiable data structure). Worth a look.

Opened as a draft for WG discussion — happy to split the `credentialStatus` point out, or to restructure if the group would rather see delegation land in a companion specification.

title: refactor(discovery)!: retire vta/discovery/capabilities — every member had a better home
body:
Closes #1043.

Follow-up to #1039, which reduced `spec/vta/discovery/capabilities/1.0` to `version` + `webvhServers` + `didCreationModes` and left the question open: **does what remains still earn a task?**

Audited each member against the rest of the surface. The answer is no — every one of them has a better home or describes nothing.

## `version` — duplicated at `GET /health/details`

`HealthDetailsResponse` already carries it, from the same `env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")`, at the same auth level (`health_details` takes `AuthClaims`).

The weakest of the three findings: both read the same constant, so unlike `services` they cannot disagree. Duplicated, not wrong.

## `webvhServers` — a *lossy* duplicate of `webvh/servers/list/1.0`

| | shape |
|---|---|
| capabilities | `WebvhServerInfo { id, label }` |
| `webvh/servers/list/1.0` | `WebvhServerRecord { id, did, label, createdAt, updatedAt }` |

Same underlying `webvh_store::list_servers` call. The dedicated task returns a strict superset.

The obvious objection is authorization — a cheap summary for callers who cannot see the full list — and **it does not hold**. `operations::did_webvh::list_webvh_servers` is commented *"Any authenticated user can list servers"*, exactly the gate capabilities used.

No production code read it from capabilities. `vtc-service/src/setup/wizard.rs` already calls `list_webvh_servers()`.

## `didCreationModes` — dead, and misleading

- **No consumer** in this repo or in OpenVTC.
- Derived entirely from `cfg!(feature = "webvh")` — the same species as the `features` booleans #1039 removed, reporting what the binary *could* do rather than what it does.
- Its vocabulary — `vta-built` / `template` / `final` / `user-specified-keys` — **appears nowhere else in the codebase**. It dates to #22 (April) and predates `WebvhPathMode`, which is the axis DID creation actually turns on now.
- The fixtures "covering" it assert `["webvh"]` — a *fourth* vocabulary, matching neither the code nor anything else. Its test coverage was fiction, the same defect class as #1033.

## Conclusion: retire the task

Every member migrates or dies:

| member | goes to |
|---|---|
| `version` | `GET /health/details` |
| `webvhServers` | `webvh/servers/list/1.0` (strict superset, same auth) |
| `didCreationModes` | nothing — it describes nothing |

This closes the `registry-drift-triage.md` row as **fold/delete**, which was its original recommendation before #1039 recorded "keep the delta".

The `discovery/1.0/*` DIDComm protocol beside it goes too — it was routed **unauthenticated**, which is worth noting on the way out.

Only consumer to migrate: `vta-mcp`'s `vta_capabilities` tool.

## On retiring rather than deprecating

`deprecation.rs` sets this repo's practice for removing a REST route — mark it, count usage, delete on an *observed zero* rather than a guessed date. **There is no equivalent for Trust Task URIs**, so that instrument is not available here.

The justification is therefore the audit above rather than a metric: zero consumers across both repos, plus a member whose vocabulary corresponds to nothing. That is a weaker instrument than the REST routes get, and worth stating rather than glossing.

If that is too weak a basis, the alternative is to build task-level deprecation signalling first — which is a larger piece of work and probably worth doing on its own merits.


---

## What the change does

Removes the task, the `discovery/1.0/*` DIDComm protocol beside it, and the types behind them: `CapabilitiesResponse`, `CapabilitiesBody`, `FeaturesInfo`, `ServicesInfo`, `WebvhServerInfo`, and `VtaClient::capabilities`.

`vta-mcp`'s `vta_capabilities` becomes **`vta_supported_tasks`**. Not a rename — the old tool promised four answers, three better held elsewhere and one describing nothing. The new description says what an agent actually needs to know before calling an operation, including that calling an unserved task fails as a *transport timeout* rather than a clear error, which is the reason to ask first.

Also discharges the `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` entry **by deletion rather than by a spec** — the cheaper way to shrink that list when the answer is "this should not exist".

## A dangling row #1042 left behind

`deprecation.rs` still carried a `GET /capabilities` row after #1042 deleted the route — matching a path that can never be hit again. **Nothing catches that**: no test ties the superseded-route table to the live router. Removed by hand here.

Worth a follow-up on its own: that table is meant to gate route removal on observed-zero usage, and a row for a route that no longer exists silently reads as "zero" forever.

## Tests

Rewritten rather than deleted, because the properties survive their subject:

- `capabilities_requires_auth` → **`trust_tasks_require_auth`**. The property was the dispatch spine's, not that task's.
- `capabilities_via_didcomm` → **`supported_trust_tasks_via_didcomm`**. Same property — a discovery answer survives the DIDComm round trip — asked of the task with a canonical answer.
- `with_didcomm_sequential_cycles_for_same_did_do_not_duel` repointed. It is about session lifecycle, not about what was asked; discovery suits because it needs no responder state.
- New: `supported_trust_tasks_decodes_without_a_framework_version`, because `frameworkVersion` is **OPTIONAL in 0.1** — an older responder omitting it must decode, not error.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` all clean.
- Full `cargo test --workspace` green except the four `vtc-service` `admin_ui::tests`, which fail on `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` leaving the embedded dir empty — the flag, not this change.
- Net **−172 lines**.

Rebased onto `main` after #1042 merged, so this is no longer stacked.

## Breaking change

Flagged as `BREAKING CHANGE:` in the commit body. Migration: `trust-task-discovery/0.1` (`VtaClient::supported_trust_tasks`) for what an agent serves, `GET /health/details` for its version, `webvh/servers/list/1.0` for its webvh hosts. No `version =` touched.

title: feat(discovery)!: serve canonical capability negotiation, drop the parallel REST route
body:
Closes #1039.

Clients had no way to ask a VTA which Trust Tasks it serves. Calling one it does not is a 30-second DIDComm timeout with no explanation — the failure mode that keeps costing us live debugging time.

**The answer already existed and we were not serving it.** `trust-task-discovery/0.1` is a published family in the dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf registry, carried by the `trust-tasks-rs` version we already depend on. A client sends slug-glob patterns (`*`, `acl/*`, or an exact slug); the responder returns the Type URIs it serves plus the framework version it targets. Nothing needed inventing, and — unusually for a new family — **nothing needed specifying upstream first**, so this was not blocked the way #1029 is.

## Answered from the dispatch table, not a list

`dispatched_uris()` was already generated by `dispatch_table!` from the same declarations that build the match arms. It is now available at runtime rather than only under `cfg(test)`, so the discovery reply cannot claim a task the service does not route.

A hand-maintained list would be a second source of truth, and an overstated discovery response is *worse* than none: a client believes a task is available and finds out on a live call.

## What this does not do

It answers **"do we both know this task, at this version"**. It does **not** answer "do we agree how its payload is spelled" — two peers can both serve `contexts/create/1.0` and still disagree about `basePath` vs `base_path`, which is exactly what #1033 was.

That's stated on the SDK method itself, because the obvious misreading is that discovery makes wire skew detectable. It doesn't, and believing it does would be worse than not having it.

## `GET /capabilities` is gone

Nothing consumed it — `VtaClient::capabilities` goes over `rpc_tt` like every other task, and no doc or downstream reads the route. A REST route running parallel to a Trust Task is precisely the shape #1020 removed everywhere else; the Trust-Task surface is already reachable over REST at `POST <base>/trust-tasks`.

Removing it also **dissolved the reason #1034 deferred folding `CapabilitiesResponse`**. The hesitation was re-casing a public discovery endpoint whose readers nobody can enumerate. With the endpoint gone, the only consumers left decode this very struct — so the fold is free, and taken here.

## Both remaining inert aliases folded

`UpdateRetentionBody` too, so `audit/update-retention` stops taking a snake_case request and returning a camelCase response — an asymmetry nobody chose, in one file, one screen apart.

This one is a **request** body, so the risk runs the other way: a client on this version sends `retentionDays`, and an agent predating the change rejects it. Same trade #1000 made for every request body it folded — taken deliberately rather than inherited from an unrelated fix.

**`INERT_BY_DECISION` is now empty**, which is the intended end state rather than a coincidence. The census still fails on any new inert alias.

## Three things worth a reviewer's eye

- **The OpenAPI assertion moved rather than went.** It was pinned on `/capabilities` as "the first route migrated to OpenAPI-aware registration". What it actually asserts is that `routes!()` registration still lands operations in the served document, and that property didn't leave with the route — so it is re-pinned on `/auth/challenge`.
- **The two `capabilities_*` integration tests now drive the Trust-Task surface.** The properties they assert — authenticated, reports features — are unchanged; only the door is.
- **A wrong assumption its own test caught.** ACL folded to the *top-level* canonical family, so the slug is `acl/grant/0.1`, not `vta/acl/grant/0.1`. My first draft of both the handler test and the conformance witness used the VTA-namespaced form. It fails **silently** — a wrong pattern returns an empty list, not an error — so the corrected unit test now asserts the negative case (`vta/acl/*` must *not* match) alongside the positive one.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` all clean.
- Full `cargo test --workspace` green except the four `vtc-service` `admin_ui::tests`, which fail on `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` leaving the embedded dir empty — the flag, not this change.
- `vta-service` lib 841/841, including the conformance sweep, which demanded and now has a witness for the new URI.
- New coverage: 5 unit tests on the pattern grammar, 2 integration tests on the live surface (narrowed query and unfiltered), plus the two rewritten capabilities tests.

## Breaking change

`GET /capabilities` is removed. `CapabilitiesResponse` and `UpdateRetentionBody` now emit lowerCamelCase, with their existing aliases accepting the retired spelling on intake. Flagged as `BREAKING CHANGE:` in the commit body; no `version =` touched.

## `features` / `services` removed too

Added on review. `CapabilitiesResponse` carried booleans for webvh / didcomm / tee / rest; both members are gone, reducing this task to exactly the delta `registry-drift-triage.md` says it should be.

The workspace already has an authority here — CLAUDE.md: **the DID document is authoritative for which protocols a party speaks**, matched on service `type`. A second answer to the same question is a second answer that can be wrong.

And these were wrong-*capable*, not merely redundant:

- **`services` read local config**, while a peer resolves the DID document. Runtime service management can change what is advertised without the config moving — so the two could disagree about precisely the thing a caller was asking.
- **`features` reported compile-time `cfg!` flags** — what the binary *could* serve, not what it does. The honest version of that question is `trust-task-discovery/0.1`, answered from the dispatch table.

`FeaturesInfo` and `ServicesInfo` are deleted; both handlers (Trust Task and DIDComm) updated.

Two test choices worth a look:

- The SDK fixture **still sends `features`/`services`** on purpose. A current agent no longer emits them, and the property being checked is that an older agent's extra members are ignored rather than rejected.
- The integration test asserts their **absence**. Asserting only the remaining members would pass whether or not the removal actually happened.

## Follow-on

`registry-drift-triage.md` is updated: its "diff `vta/discovery/capabilities` against the published family" item is now **done**, and resolves to *keep, spec the delta* — webvh hosts and DID-creation modes genuinely exceed what discovery covers, and with `features`/`services` gone that is all this task carries.

title: Two deferred casing folds: CapabilitiesResponse (REST surface) and UpdateRetentionBody (request direction)
body:
Split out of #1034, which folded `SeedInfo` and left these two. Both carry inert `serde` aliases from #1000 — attributes that accept only what would be accepted anyway, because the container never got the `rename_all` they were written to accompany. Both are held by `INERT_BY_DECISION` in `vta-sdk/tests/inert_alias_census.rs`, so neither can be forgotten and neither can be quietly "fixed" by deleting the alias.

`SeedInfo` was safe to finish because its **containing body was already folded** — `seeds/list` was emitting `{"seeds":[{"created_at":…}],"activeSeedId":1}`, a body that disagreed with itself. Neither type below has moved at all, so folding either is a **fresh wire change**, not the completion of a half-done one. That distinction is the whole reason they are here.

## 1. `CapabilitiesResponse`

`vta-sdk/src/protocols/discovery.rs:21` — `webvh_servers`, `did_creation_modes`.

Served on **three** surfaces: the `discovery/capabilities/1.0` Trust Task, the DIDComm handler, and the REST route `GET /capabilities` (`vta-service/src/routes/capabilities.rs`).

The REST surface is the problem. #1000 deliberately deferred REST bodies:

> REST request/response bodies (`routes/`, `client/types.rs`, `protocol/`) are a further 54 structs with the same problem. They are left for a separate change: unlike task payloads, no published schema pins their casing, and changing what they emit breaks readers that have no alias to fall back on.

`/capabilities` is a discovery endpoint — precisely the kind a third-party tool reads. Nothing in this repo or its docs consumes the snake_case spelling (the SDK shares the struct), but that is not proof of absence.

`spec/vta/discovery/capabilities/1.0` is in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`, so no generated consumer expects camelCase either. There is no correctness forcing function — only §4.10 consistency.

## 2. `UpdateRetentionBody`

`vta-sdk/src/protocols/audit_management/retention.rs:14` — `retention_days`.

**Found by the census, not by anyone reading the file**, which is the strongest argument for having built it.

It is the clearest miss of the three. One screen down in the same file, `RetentionResultBody` **is** folded, and even the empty `GetRetentionBody` carries `rename_all`. So `audit/update-retention` currently takes a **snake_case request** and returns a **camelCase response**. Nobody chose that.

Deferred anyway, because it is a **request** body. Folding it changes what clients *send* — on the Trust-Task, DIDComm and REST surfaces at once — and an agent that predates the change rejects the new spelling with `malformedRequest`. That is the opposite direction from `SeedInfo`, where a new agent's output is absorbed by aliases the client already has.

The hazard is not novel: #1000 made the same trade for every request body it folded. But it is a cross-version break between our own components, and it deserves to be taken deliberately rather than inherited from a census fix.

## Requested

For each, decide and then act:

- **Fold** — add `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]`, which activates the aliases already present, and drop the entry from `INERT_BY_DECISION`.
- **Or record it as settled** — keep snake_case as the wire for that surface and say so in the entry's reason, which is what `INERT_BY_DECISION` is for.

Do **not** resolve either by deleting the alias. The alias is the only thing that will let an older producer keep working once the fold lands; removing it makes the eventual fold a hard break instead of a Postel one.

## Ordering note

`UpdateRetentionBody` is the better first move despite being a request body: it is unambiguously an oversight, its blast radius is one operator-facing command (`pnm audit retention set`), and fixing it makes one task internally consistent. `CapabilitiesResponse` is better handled together with the wider REST-body fold #1000 deferred, rather than as a one-off.

## Acceptance

- `INERT_BY_DECISION` is empty, or every remaining entry states a decision rather than a delay.
- `inert_alias_census.rs` stays green — including `the_exception_list_has_no_stale_entries`, which fails if a type is folded but its entry is left behind.
- If `CapabilitiesResponse` is folded, `vta-service/tests/api_integration.rs:328` (`body["did_creation_modes"]`) moves with it.

body:
feat(discovery)!: serve canonical capability negotiation, drop the parallel REST route (#1042)

* feat(discovery)!: serve canonical capability negotiation, drop the parallel REST route

Clients had no way to ask a VTA which Trust Tasks it serves. Calling one it does
not is a 30-second DIDComm timeout with no explanation — the failure mode
`didhosting-083-retired-task-uris` describes.

The answer already existed and we were not serving it. `trust-task-discovery/0.1`
is a published family in the dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf registry, carried by the

the framework version it targets. Nothing needed inventing, and — unusually for a
new family — nothing needed specifying upstream first.

The VTA answers **from its own dispatch table**. `dispatched_uris()` was already
generated by `dispatch_table!` from the same declarations that build the match
arms; it is now available at runtime rather than only under `cfg(test)`. A
hand-maintained list would be a second source of truth, and an overstated
discovery response is worse than none: a client believes a task is available and
finds out on a live call.

**What this does not do.** It answers "do we both know this task, at this
version". It does not answer "do we agree how its payload is spelled" — two peers
can both serve `contexts/create/1.0` and still disagree about `basePath` vs

title: Use did:webvh in examples and state what each VID role needs of a DID method
body:
## Summary

Two related changes to how this specification treats DID methods.

**The examples showed `did:web` for durable issuers.** The VTC (`chess-club.example`), the witness service, and the IDVC issuer were all `did:web`. That method resolves to a document with no verifiable history: a verifier can establish which key is authoritative *now*, but not which key was authoritative *when the credential was signed*, and there is no recovery path on key compromise. Since DTG credentials may be presented long after issuance, and [Security Considerations](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#security-considerations) requires verifiers to validate the verification method, `did:web` understates what the specification assumes of a C-DID.

These examples now use [`did:webvh`](https://identity.foundation/didwebvh/), whose DID log publishes an append-only history of document versions, commits to successor keys via `nextKeyHashes`, and may be witnessed. Pairwise subjects are unchanged and stay on `did:key` / `did:peer`.

**The specification was silent on what it needs from a DID method.** It mandates none — correctly, and this PR does not change that — but it also never said what it relies on a method to provide, leaving implementers no basis for choosing one. The new informative `DID Method Considerations` subsection separates the two property sets, which pull against each other:

| | Durable (C-DID, M-DID) | Pairwise (R-DID, P-DID) |
|---|---|---|
| Key history | Verifiable, so signing-time key state is recoverable | Not required |
| Rotation | Without changing the identifier | Not required |
| Successor keys | Pre-rotation or equivalent commitment | Not required |
| Creation cost | Amortised over the identifier's life | Cheap, no registration step |
| Resolution origin | Independent of a single operator | **Not shared across identifiers** |
| Service endpoints | Discoverable (VTA, `credentialStatus`, trust registry) | Not required |

The conclusion is that implementations should expect to use more than one method rather than seeking one that serves every role. Nothing here requires an `issuer` and a `credentialSubject.id` to share a method, and the examples now reflect that.

## Privacy consideration 7

Correlation does not require the credentials themselves. Where several of a party's R-DIDs or P-DIDs resolve through common infrastructure — a shared web origin, a shared registry, or a shared set of witnesses observing their updates — that infrastructure can associate identifiers the credential structure was designed to keep apart, and can observe when each is used.

The existing considerations (1–3) cover correlation through credential *content*; none covered correlation through the *resolution layer*. This makes DID method choice for pairwise roles a privacy decision, not only a key management one — and it is the reason the table above marks "no shared resolution origin" as the property that distinguishes the two sets.

## Notes for reviewers

- **Entirely informative.** No normative requirement is added, changed, or removed. No schema changes.
- **No method is mandated.** `did:webvh` appears in examples and as an illustration of a method satisfying the durable-role properties; the text is written in terms of properties so that other methods can be assessed against it. This is deliberate — it is what makes a later conformance statement for, say, a KERI-based method cheap to write.
- **SCIDs in the examples are illustrative placeholders**, truncated in the house style used elsewhere for `did:key` and `did:peer` values. They are not real, resolvable SCIDs.
- Independent of #19; the two touch different parts of the document.

title: chore(deps): vta-sdk 0.27, trust-tasks 0.11, and one sdk in the binary again
body:
**Zero source changes.** Two `vta-sdk` minors were crossed and nothing here broke — which is worth stating, because the 0.22→0.23 and 0.24→0.25 moves each broke exactly one struct literal. Manifests and the lockfile, and that is all.

Two commits: the sdk line, then the `did-git-sign` floor that VGI had to publish before this repo could take it.

## What moves

| requirement | from | to |
|---|---|---|
| `vta-sdk` | 0.25 | **0.27** |
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.9 | **0.11** |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.8 | **0.9** |
| `vta-service` (**dev**-dependency) | 0.17 | **0.19** |
| `affinidi-messaging-sdk` | 0.19.4 | **0.19.9** |
| `affinidi-messaging-delivery` | 0.1.12 | **0.1.14** |
| `affinidi-tdk` | 0.8 | 0.8.5 |
| `agent-names` | 0.1.2 | 0.1.3 |

The first four cannot move independently: `vta-sdk` 0.27 declares `trust-tasks-rs ^0.11`, `trust-tasks-capability-client` re-exports the same `TrustTask`, and `vta-service` 0.19 is the line built on `vta-sdk` 0.27. Any one held back is a second semver-incompatible copy of a type that crosses the sdk boundary.

`affinidi-tdk` 0.8.5 and `agent-names` 0.1.3 are floors **by construction** — both are `vta-sdk` 0.27's own requirements. The manifest now says so rather than implying the older versions are still viable.

## A third crate has to follow trust-tasks, not just `vta-service`

`affinidi-messaging-sdk` carries `trust-tasks-rs` types in its own public API — `acl_setup.rs` hands a `MediatorAcl` built from its own copy into `atm.trust_tasks().account_update`. A copy left on 0.9 is not untidy, it is `expected MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`.

So its floor goes to **0.19.9**, the release where affinidi-tdk-rs #717 moves the messaging crates to 0.11. This is easy to miss because it reads as an unrelated transport dependency — same shape as the `vta-service` trap #229 documented, where the crate that reintroduces the duplicate is never the one you set out to bump.

## Three floors that are live defect fixes

**`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19.8 — the listener flapping we chased for weeks.** tdk #716: `_refresh_authentication` discarded `force_refresh`, so the websocket transport's proactive refresh at 80% of token life rebuilt the socket *without* refreshing and re-armed at 80% of the time **remaining**. A geometric cascade of reconnects per token instead of one clean cycle — the symptom #231–#234 saw as two listeners flapping every ~15 minutes. The lockfile has carried it since #232; the **floor** did not, so a clean checkout could resolve straight back onto the storm.

**`affinidi-messaging-delivery` 0.1.14 — messages destroyed, not delayed.** tdk #710: the dispatcher acked every inbound message unconditionally, and an ack is a **delete at the mediator** — including when `subscribers.send` had just reported nobody listening. No subscriber is installed for a moment at startup and again on the way down. For this repo the contents of those windows are a membership credential or a join reply: exactly the class of loss #218's pickup-on-connect exists to prevent, being undone one layer below it.

**`vta-sdk` 0.27.0 — a silent degradation on our own call sites.** VTI #1033: #1000 folded Trust-Task payloads to lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10 but excluded `client/types.rs` on a stale path assumption, so the agent moved to `basePath` while the client went on demanding `base_path` — eleven required fields with no `default`, across `contexts` create/get/update/list and `keys` sign/rename/revoke/export-secret.

Both our `list_contexts()` call sites sit behind `let Ok(..)`/`match` (`state_handler/mod.rs:766`, `openvtc-core/src/context_probe.rs:137`), so against a post-#1000 agent this never surfaced as an error — the sub-context probe simply saw nothing. The fix is intake **aliases** rather than a rename, so 0.27 still decodes an older agent's snake_case: safe against a VTA on either side of the fold.

## Also in 0.26, not adopted

VTI #1012 adds `VtaClient::idempotent`, which holds one `idempotencyKey` across every attempt of an operation so a retried `create_key` is deduplicated at the VTA rather than taking effect twice. Our retry owner is still `vta_retry()`. Left alone here — but it is the seam that should replace it, and the manifest note records that so it is not rediscovered from scratch.

0.26 is also **not a viable floor**: it declares `trust-tasks-rs ^0.9`, so a checkout resolving back to it while this workspace is on 0.11 puts two `trust-tasks-rs` in the binary — the same trap 0.24 (`^0.6`) posed against 0.9 and 0.23.0 (`^0.4`) posed against 0.6.

## The other half: `did-git-sign` had to be released first

`did-git-sign` 0.4.5 requires `vta-sdk ^0.25`, so moving this workspace to 0.27 left the published signer dragging the old line back in through a single edge:

```
vta-sdk v0.25.1
└── did-git-sign v0.4.5
    └── openvtc v0.3.1
```

**Third cycle running** — the same position #229 described before VGI 0.4.5, and #216 before that. OpenVTC/verifiable-git-infrastructure#32 published **0.4.6** on `vta-sdk` 0.27, and the second commit here takes it. `cargo update -p did-git-sign` states the result plainly:

```
Updating did-git-sign v0.4.5 -> v0.4.6
Removing trust-tasks-rs v0.9.0
Updating vgi-core v0.4.5 -> v0.4.6
Removing vta-sdk v0.25.1
```

### Why the requirement names 0.4.6 rather than staying on a caret

`"0.4.3"` already admitted 0.4.5 — that is exactly how the duplicate arrived while this line looked untouched. A caret permitting any release built on an older sdk lets a clean checkout resolve straight back onto the second copy, with nothing in the manifest to say it happened. The floor has to name the release that is actually on the current sdk line.

The comment also records why this particular duplicate never broke a build, because the reason is narrow and should not be read as safety: we use only `did_git_sign::{config, init}`, so no type crosses the boundary. One new import is all it would take — `vti-common` re-exports `vta_sdk::acl::{ActScope, ApproveScope, ContextDirection}` as its own public API, so the copies do carry types that cannot unify.

Note VGI still holds `trust-tasks-rs` 0.9 via `trql-client` → `verify-trust` (the trust registry has published nothing on 0.11 yet). That does **not** reach here: `did-git-sign` has no trql-client edge. Documented on both sides.

## Comments updated

Every block that moved now records **this** move rather than the last one, and older satisfied floors are dropped to git history rather than kept as a wall of constraints. New notes: why `affinidi-messaging-sdk` is a trust-tasks follower, why 0.26 is not a floor, and the standing cross-repo obligation on `did-git-sign` — written once, in that crate's floor note, with the root `vta-sdk` block pointing at it rather than describing it twice.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — pass
- `cargo test --workspace --no-default-features` — pass
- `cargo test -p openvtc-core --features arbitrary --lib` — 430 pass
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` — clean (a separate lint set from clippy, and its own CI gate)
- `cargo test --workspace -- --ignored` — pass, including `mockvta_bootstrap_e2e`, `join_lifecycle_e2e` and `relationship_e2e`. These are the only thing here that actually exercises **`vta-service` 0.19**; plain `cargo test --workspace` skips every one of them.
- `cargo outdated --root-deps-only` — *"All dependencies are up to date"*
- `cargo tree -d -e normal,build,dev` — lists **none** of `vta-sdk`, `vta-service`, `trust-tasks-rs`, `trust-tasks-capability-client`, `vti-common`, `affinidi-tdk`, `dtg-credentials`, `didwebvh-rs`, `agent-names`, `did-git-sign` or `vgi-core`
- `cargo tree -i vta-sdk` — a single **0.27.0** node, with all four consumers (`openvtc`, `openvtc-core`, `did-git-sign`, `vta-service`) on it

The full gate was re-run after the second commit, not just the first.

`affinidi-messaging-delivery`'s floor goes 0.1.12 -> 0.1.14 for the same reason
— affinidi-tdk-rs #710. The dispatcher acked every inbound message
unconditionally, and an ack is a *delete* at the mediator, including when
`subscribers.send` had just reported nobody listening. No subscriber is
installed for a moment at startup and again on the way down, so what arrived in
those windows was destroyed. For this repo that is a membership credential or a
join reply — the class of loss #218's pickup-on-connect exists to prevent, being
undone one layer below it.

`affinidi-tdk` 0.8 -> 0.8.5 and `agent-names` 0.1.2 -> 0.1.3 are floors by
construction: both are `vta-sdk` 0.27's own requirements, and the manifest now
says so rather than implying the older versions are still viable.

## What the sdk bump buys

Nothing broke. Two minors were crossed and the workspace compiled, tested and
documented clean with no source change — which is worth stating, because the
0.24 -> 0.25 and 0.22 -> 0.23 moves each broke exactly one struct literal.

VTI #1033 (0.27.0) is the reason to take it. #1000 folded Trust-Task payloads to
lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10 but excluded `client/types.rs` on a stale path
assumption, so the agent moved to `basePath` while the client went on demanding
`base_path` — eleven required fields with no `default`, across `contexts`
create/get/update/list and `keys` sign/rename/revoke/export-secret. Both our
`list_contexts()` call sites sit behind `let Ok(..)`/`match`
(`state_handler/mod.rs`, `context_probe.rs`), so against a post-#1000 agent this
degraded silently rather than erroring: the sub-context probe simply saw
nothing. The fix is intake aliases rather than a rename, so 0.27 still decodes
an older agent's snake_case — safe against a VTA on either side of the fold.

VTI #1012 (0.26.0) adds `VtaClient::idempotent`, which holds one
`idempotencyKey` across every attempt so a retried `create_key` is deduplicated
at the VTA rather than taking effect twice. Not adopted here — `vta_retry()` is
still our retry owner — but it is the seam that should replace it, and the note
in the manifest records that.

## The duplicate that remains

`cargo tree -d -e normal,build,dev` reports `vta-sdk` 0.25.1 and
`trust-tasks-rs` 0.9.0 alongside the new lines. Both are reached through exactly
one edge:

    vta-sdk v0.25.1
    └── did-git-sign v0.4.5
        └── openvtc v0.3.1

`did-git-sign` 0.4.5 requires `vta-sdk ^0.25`, and this repo's graph is once
again pinned by a dependency two repos away — the same position #229 described
before VGI 0.4.5 unblocked it. It builds and tests clean because no type crosses
that boundary: we use only `did_git_sign::{config, init}`. It clears when VGI
cuts a release on 0.27, at which point `did-git-sign`'s requirement here must be
raised to that version rather than left at the `"0.4.3"` caret, or a fresh
checkout resolves straight back onto 0.25.

## Verification

`cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features
-- -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`, `cargo test --workspace
--no-default-features`, `cargo test -p openvtc-core --features arbitrary --lib`
and `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` all pass. The
`#[ignore]`d e2e suites — the ones that boot the in-process `MockVta`, and so the
only thing here that actually exercises `vta-service` 0.19 — were run with
`cargo test --workspace -- --ignored` and pass, including the bootstrap,
join-lifecycle and relationship round-trips.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* chore(deps): floor did-git-sign at 0.4.6, leaving one vta-sdk in the binary

The other half of the preceding commit, and the half this repo cannot supply
itself. `did-git-sign` 0.4.5 requires `vta-sdk ^0.25`, so moving the workspace to
0.27 left the published signer dragging the old line back in through a single
edge:

    vta-sdk v0.25.1
    └── did-git-sign v0.4.5
        └── openvtc v0.3.1

VGI #32 published 0.4.6 on `vta-sdk` 0.27, which closes it. `cargo update -p
did-git-sign` says so in as many words:

    Updating did-git-sign v0.4.5 -> v0.4.6
    Removing trust-tasks-rs v0.9.0
    Updating vgi-core v0.4.5 -> v0.4.6
    Removing vta-sdk v0.25.1

## Why the requirement names 0.4.6 rather than staying on a caret

`"0.4.3"` already admitted 0.4.5 — that is exactly how the duplicate arrived
while this line looked untouched. A caret that permits any release built on an
older sdk lets a clean checkout resolve straight back onto the second copy, with
nothing in the manifest to say it happened. The floor has to name the release
that is actually on the current sdk line.

This is the third consecutive cycle the same note has been rewritten — 0.4.3 was
the first release on 0.23, 0.4.5 the first on 0.25, 0.4.6 the first on 0.27 — so
it now reads as a standing obligation rather than an incident report: when this
workspace's `vta-sdk` minor moves, VGI has to publish before this line can
follow, and until it does the graph carries two sdks.

The comment also records why this particular duplicate never broke a build,
because the reason is narrow and should not be mistaken for safety: we use only
`did_git_sign::{config, init}`, so no type crosses the boundary. One new import
is all it would take. `vti-common` re-exports `vta_sdk::acl::{ActScope,
ApproveScope, ContextDirection}` as its own public API, so the two copies do
carry types that cannot unify.

The `vta-sdk` note in the root manifest loses its "one consumer still holds this
graph back" paragraph and gains a pointer to the floor note instead, so the
obligation is written in one place rather than described twice.

## Verification

`cargo tree -d -e normal,build,dev` now lists none of `vta-sdk`, `vta-service`,
`trust-tasks-rs`, `trust-tasks-capability-client`, `vti-common`, `affinidi-tdk`,
`dtg-credentials`, `didwebvh-rs`, `agent-names`, `did-git-sign` or `vgi-core`,
and `cargo tree -i vta-sdk` resolves a single 0.27.0 node with all four
consumers — `openvtc`, `openvtc-core`, `did-git-sign` and `vta-service` — on it.

`cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features
-- -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`, `cargo test --workspace -- --ignored`
(the MockVta e2e suites) and `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace
--no-deps` all pass.

title: docs: design note for the application-state store
body:
Refs #1029. **Design only** — no code, no URIs registered, nothing dispatched.

Adds `docs/05-design-notes/appstate-store.md` and indexes it in `docs/README.md`.

## Why a note before code

#1029 cannot be built first and specified afterwards, and that is not a style preference — the dispatcher enforces it. `every_served_uri_has_a_published_spec_or_is_tracked_debt` fails on any served URI the published registry has no schema for, and its own assertion says what to do instead:

> Author the spec upstream in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf and bump trust-tasks-rs — growing the allowlist is the wrong fix.

So the first deliverable is a schema **in another repository**, and this note is its input.

**Worth knowing before this is scheduled:** the implementation is a few days; the sequencing is not. Steps 1–2 below are on another team's cadence.

1. Author `spec/vta/appstate/{get,put,list,delete,get-many,put-many}/1.0` upstream
2. Bump `trust-tasks-rs` so `schema_index::schema_for` resolves them — until this lands, step 3 cannot pass its own test suite
3. Implement here — keyspace, storage, operations, dispatch, `retry_safety`, conformance witnesses, SDK
4. OpenVTC adopts

## What the note settles

**Why not the three existing stores**, verified against the source rather than restated from the issue. `MemoryItem` really is `{key, value}` with no version, and `MemoryListResponse` really does document itself as returning *"every entry in the context"* with no prefix or cursor. The settling argument is the one that is easy to skip past: **"forget everything" is a reasonable thing to ask an agent, and it must not delete your community memberships.**

**What to reuse rather than reinvent** — the part most likely to be got wrong by someone starting from the issue alone:

- `vti_common::pagination` is the workspace-wide cursor standard (opaque, HMAC-signed, shared `paginate()`); the VTA signs under `CursorKey` because it has no audit chain. A bespoke offset would be both a regression and a second thing to get wrong.
- Idempotency is generic at the dispatch spine, driven by `retry_safety` — where a census test means a new task cannot be added without someone classifying it.
- `MEMORY` is the keyspace precedent for everything but the semantics: per-context, prefix-scanned, `BACKED_UP` as *"durable user data"*. `appstate` differs only by a namespace segment and a version, so `list` with a `prefix` narrows the existing scan rather than adding an access pattern.

**Proposed retry classifications**, including the one that needs saying out loud: `put` should be `Keyed` even though supplying `expectedVersion` makes *that* call converge. The class is per-URI, not per-payload, and `retry_safety`'s own rule is to classify conservatively where convergence is not obvious from the contract. Stated so a future reader does not "optimise" it on the strength of the precondition.

## A correction to the issue

#1029 says the `backup_export_via_descriptor` → `download_blob` path is *"documented REST-only, and OpenVTC speaks DIDComm"*. The code says something sharper: a DIDComm or TSP client **can** use it, through an optional `rest_client` side-channel —

```rust
Transport::DIDComm { rest_client, .. } => rest_client.as_ref().ok_or_else(|| {
    VtaError::Validation("DIDComm transport has no REST client for blob download".into())
})?,
```

— which is `Some` exactly when the client knows a REST URL (`client/mod.rs:457`).

**The real constraint is deployment-shaped, not transport-shaped.** A VTA may legitimately stop advertising REST: runtime service management allows disabling a transport provided one remains, so a DIDComm-or-TSP-only VTA is supported. On such a VTA the blob path is unreachable — meaning blobs would work on some deployments and not others, with no signal.

Three ways out are set out. **Recommendation: defer blobs.** Nothing in the stated OpenVTC need — labels, relationships, contacts, join history — obviously wants one, the rest of the design is sound and unblocked without them, and deferring keeps a REST-advertisement decision off the critical path for account recovery.

## Open questions (§8)

Five, each stated with why it is cheaper to answer now than later. The two worth flagging here:

- **Are namespaces a trust boundary or a collision-avoidance convention?** The address supports per-namespace ACLs; nothing grants them. Answering "trust boundary" later is a migration, so it is worth answering now even if the answer is "not yet".
- **Is `appstate` the right name?** It is the issue's noun, but neighbouring task families hyphenate. After the URIs are published a rename is a new family, not a rename.

Docs-only; no crate source touched, so no version bump (VTI assigns those in the release PR).

title: fix(sdk): finish the seeds/list fold, and make an inert alias fail the build
body:
Closes #1034. Refs #1039.

`seeds/list` emitted a body that disagreed with itself:

```json
{"seeds":[{"id":1,"status":"active","created_at":"…"}],"activeSeedId":1}
```

#1000 folded Trust Task payloads to lowerCamelCase and gave 126 members an `alias` for the retired spelling. `SeedInfo` got the aliases and **not** the `rename_all` that gives them meaning — and an alias equal to the member's own name is a no-op — so it kept emitting snake_case while `ListSeedsResultBody` around it moved.

Adding the `rename_all` finishes that fold and activates the aliases, so a producer still sending `created_at` keeps decoding.

**Safe to finish precisely because the containing body already moved.** The same REST route (`GET /keys/seeds`) has emitted `activeSeedId` since #1000, and since #1035 the client's `SeedInfoResponse` *is* `SeedInfo`, so both ends move together.

## The class, not the instances

An inert alias is not untidiness — it is how this shipped. The code compiled, every test passed, and the attribute reads as though the work was done; a reviewer seeing `alias = "created_at"` reasonably assumes the member is now `createdAt`. Both known instances were found **by hand, months later, while auditing something else**.

`vta-sdk/tests/inert_alias_census.rs` decides it from the source instead, for every wire type under `protocols/` at once.

**Verified non-vacuous in every direction** — each guard was proven by making it fail, not assumed:

| Guard | Injected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Catches the original bug | reverted this PR's `rename_all` | reports `SeedInfo.created_at` + `.retired_at` — **red** |
| Catches a new one | inert alias added to an already-folded struct | reports it by file, struct, field — **red** |
| Allow-list can't rot | entry for a type that no longer needs one | reports it as stale — **red** |
| Not scanning nothing | — | floors on files scanned **and** aliases parsed |

That last floor matters: a `syn` upgrade that stopped understanding these attributes would otherwise leave the census green over an empty set — which is the exact failure mode (#1033) that started this whole thread.

## It immediately found a third instance

`UpdateRetentionBody.retention_days` — which nobody knew about, and which is the clearest miss of the three. One screen down **in the same file**, `RetentionResultBody` *is* folded, and even the empty `GetRetentionBody` carries `rename_all`. So `audit/update-retention` currently takes a **snake_case request** and returns a **camelCase response**.

## What is deferred, and why the line is where it is

Both remaining instances are recorded in `INERT_BY_DECISION` with their reasons and tracked in #1039. The distinction is whether folding **completes a change already made** or **starts a new one**:

- **`SeedInfo`** — containing body already moved. Finishing it removes an inconsistency. ✅ done here.
- **`CapabilitiesResponse`** — has not moved at all, and is served on `GET /capabilities` as well as the Trust-Task and DIDComm surfaces. Folding is a fresh REST wire change of exactly the kind #1000 explicitly deferred.
- **`UpdateRetentionBody`** — a **request** body. Folding changes what clients *send*, and an agent predating the change rejects the new spelling. That is the opposite direction from `SeedInfo`, where a new agent's output is absorbed by aliases the client already holds.

**Deleting an inert alias is the wrong repair in every case**, and the census says so at the point where someone would try it: the alias is the only thing that lets an older producer keep working once the fold lands.

## Fixtures

The `client_rest.rs` seeds fixture is re-cut. It carried a comment (added in #1033) explaining that `seeds[]` was snake_case inside a camelCase `activeSeedId` *because that was what the agent really emitted*. That asymmetry is gone, so describing it would now be the fiction.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` all clean.
- Full `cargo test --workspace`: every target green except the four `vtc-service` `admin_ui::tests`, which fail on `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` leaving the embedded dir empty — the flag, not this change.
- New census 3/3, and confirmed running under CI's feature set alongside `trust_task_decode` (4/4) and `trust_task_decode_census` (3/3).
- No conformance witness exists for `seeds/list` (the URI is in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`), and `api_integration.rs` asserts only `body["seeds"].is_array()`, so no server-side fixture pinned the old nested spelling.

title: Dead serde aliases: two payload structs still emit snake_case after #1000
body:
## Summary

Two payload structs received `#[serde(alias = "...")]` attributes in #1000 **without** the `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` that gives them meaning. The aliases are therefore inert, and both types still emit snake_case — the exact thing that PR set out to fix.

Neither is a break today, because in both cases the agent and the client decode the *same* struct, so the two ends cannot disagree. They are a **SPEC §4.10 conformance gap**: a consumer generated from the published schema expects lowerCamelCase and will not get it.

Found while auditing all 61 `rpc_tt` call sites for #1033.

## `CapabilitiesResponse`

`vta-sdk/src/protocols/discovery.rs:21`

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct CapabilitiesResponse {          // <- no rename_all
    pub version: String,
    pub features: FeaturesInfo,
    pub services: ServicesInfo,
    #[serde(alias = "webvh_servers")]      // <- inert: the field name IS webvh_servers
    pub webvh_servers: Vec<WebvhServerInfo>,
    #[serde(alias = "did_creation_modes")] // <- inert
    pub did_creation_modes: Vec<String>,
}
```

An alias equal to the field's own serialized name is a no-op. `discovery/capabilities/1.0` still emits `webvh_servers` / `did_creation_modes`.

## `SeedInfo`

`vta-sdk/src/protocols/seed_management/list.rs:14`

Same shape — `alias = "created_at"` and `alias = "retired_at"` on fields already spelled that way, no `rename_all`. Note the *containing* type `ListSeedsResultBody` **was** folded, so `seeds/list/1.0` currently emits a half-camelCase body:

```json
{"seeds":[{"id":1,"status":"active","created_at":"..."}],"activeSeedId":1}
```

That asymmetry is real and is pinned by a fixture comment in `vta-sdk/tests/client_rest.rs::list_seeds_returns_active` — a uniform fixture would describe an agent that does not exist.

## Why this was not folded into #1033

#1033 fixed a live outage by adding aliases to the *client's* decode types. Adding `rename_all` to these two **changes what the agent emits**, which is a different kind of change and wants its own release note.

## Requested

Add `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` to both, keeping the per-field aliases (which then stop being no-ops and start doing the Postel job they were written for).

Two things must move in the same change or it will break:

1. **`SeedInfoResponse` in `vta-sdk/src/client/types.rs`** already carries `alias = "createdAt"` / `alias = "retiredAt"`, added pre-emptively in #1033 for exactly this. Verify, do not assume — `vta-sdk/tests/trust_task_decode.rs::seeds_list_decodes_including_its_elements` asserts the nested timestamp and will fail loudly if the pairing is wrong.
2. **The `client_rest.rs` fixture** and its comment describing the asymmetry become stale the moment `SeedInfo` folds, and should be re-cut in the same PR.

## Acceptance

- `discovery/capabilities/1.0` and `seeds/list/1.0` emit lowerCamelCase throughout.
- The conformance witnesses for both are updated and still non-vacuous.
- `trust_task_decode.rs` stays green — that is the check that the client half moved too.
- A snake_case body from an older producer still decodes (the aliases now doing real work).

title: refactor(sdk)!: one wire, one type — decode the agent's own bodies
body:
Closes #1035.

#1033 fixed eleven Trust-Task call sites where the client's decode type had drifted from the agent's body — breaking every `pnm contexts` command, four `pnm keys` commands, seed rotate/list, and the MCP surface. It fixed them with `serde` aliases, which restores compatibility without removing the hazard: the wire still had **two structs**, and either could move alone again.

The audit behind #1033 found the correlation was total. Of 61 call sites, the 50 decoding a shared `protocols::**` type were all fine; all 11 with a private type in `client/types.rs` were broken. That is not a coincidence to test around — it is the defect.

## What changed

Each of the eight duplicates is now a `pub use` of the body the agent serializes:

| client name (unchanged) | now refers to |
|---|---|
| `ContextResponse` | `context_management::create::CreateContextResultBody` |
| `ContextListResponse` | `context_management::list::ListContextsResultBody` |
| `SignResponse` | `key_management::sign::SignResultBody` |
| `RenameKeyResponse` | `key_management::rename::RenameKeyResultBody` |
| `InvalidateKeyResponse` | `key_management::revoke::RevokeKeyResultBody` |
| `GetKeySecretResponse` | `key_management::secret::GetKeySecretResultBody` |
| `RotateSeedResponse` | `seed_management::rotate::RotateSeedResultBody` |
| `ListSeedsResponse` / `SeedInfoResponse` | `seed_management::list::{ListSeedsResultBody, SeedInfo}` |

The client-facing names are kept, so `get_context` still returns something called `ContextResponse` rather than `CreateContextResultBody`. Two ends cannot disagree when there is one end — a stronger guarantee than any test could give.

## Two bugs a field-by-field mirror was hiding

**`vta contexts create --parent x` rendered no parent.** `bootstrap_cli.rs` carried an adapter whose own comment claimed the two types were "identical on the wire". They were not — the client struct had no `parent`, so the adapter dropped it on every offline context render. The compiler found it the moment the re-export landed:

```
error[E0063]: missing field `parent` in initializer of `ContextResponse`
   --> vta-service/src/bootstrap_cli.rs:782:5
```

Deleting the adapter fixes it.

**`{:?}` on a key-secret response printed the raw private key.** The client's `GetKeySecretResponse` derived `Debug`. The agent's `GetKeySecretResultBody` hand-writes `Debug` to redact `private_key_multibase`, specifically so a caller cannot tracing-log it by accident. Sharing the type inherits the redaction.

## What deliberately stays two types

**The ACL pair.** `AclEntryResponse` renames `subject`→`did` and `scopes`→`allowed_contexts` and converts RFC 3339 to the epoch seconds the CLI speaks. It is an adapter with real logic, not a mirror, so it cannot be re-exported. It keeps its seam cases — and that matters more now, because an adapter that *computes* can be wrong in ways a copy cannot.

**Request builders.** `CreateKeyRequest` and friends exist for ergonomics (`.new(..).label(..)`) and *produce* the wire shape rather than describing it, so they cannot drift this way.

## The tests shrink, on purpose

Nine cases in `trust_task_decode.rs` are deleted. They serialized the agent's body and decoded it into the client's type; with one type on both sides, that now asserts `serde` round-trips a type through itself — true of every type everywhere, and no longer a fact about this codebase.

Keeping them as reassurance would be keeping exactly the kind of vacuous assertion that let `acl/update` ship broken through three PRs (#856). What remains is still real: the ACL adapter, and the legacy snake_case direction — the latter arguably stronger than before, since it now exercises the intake aliases on the **agent's** types, where every consumer's backward compatibility comes from rather than just this client's.

`COVERED_BY_SEAM_TEST` drops from nine names to one. That is the shape the census was built for: the list shrinks as duplicates are removed, rather than growing as they are papered over.

**The census was re-verified after the collapse**, not assumed — re-injecting a fresh client-private decode type still fails it by name (`probe_temp -> ProbeResponse`). Its empty-scan floor still holds.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` all clean.
- Full `cargo test --workspace`: every target green except the four `vtc-service` `admin_ui::tests`, which fail on the `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` flag leaving the embedded dir empty — the flag, not this change.
- Net −178 lines.

That break is the point — the one such site in this workspace was silently dropping a member. Flagged as `BREAKING CHANGE:` in the commit body; no `version =` touched.

## Follow-on

#1034 (dead `serde` aliases on `SeedInfo` / `CapabilitiesResponse`) gets easier from here: `SeedInfoResponse` is now the same type as `SeedInfo`, so folding it moves both ends at once with nothing on this side to forget.
